items.note: Jayasimha lost his life and Malwa was conquered; Caulukyas and Karnātas took the imperial city of Dhārā, the crisis before Udayāditya.
Hoysala inscription mentions the city 'Udhapuram'; editor: 'Udhapuram may be the same as Udayapur, in the Gwalior State, Central India.'
Prthvīrāja-vijaya and Arisimha report Karna's conquest of Mālava and that he despoiled the Mālava king of an image of Nīlakaṇṭha (Śiva).
A fragmentary 1513 A.D. inscription states that Udayāditya built the temple of Udayapur in V.S. 1116 = 1059 A.D.; the record is 'perfunctorily executed' and 'abounds in gross mistakes'.

claim.value: 1059 A.D. (V.S. 1116), per a fragmentary 1513 A.D. record of doubtful quality

items.note: Ganguly reconciles 1059 with Udayāditya not yet being sovereign: he built the temple 'when he was ruling his paternal territory apparently from Udayapur'.
Udayāditya, 'a scion of a junior branch of the Paramāras', sought help from Cāhamāna Durlabha III and regained the country from the Caulukyas and Karnātas.
Per the Prthvīrāja-vijaya, Udayāditya received cavalry from Durlabha, defeated the Gurjara Kārṇa and obtained Mālava.
Quotes the Udayapur prasasti on Bhoja's death, the darkness of foes, and 'king Udayāditya, as it were another sun'.
Nagpur inscription: when Bhoja had become Indra's companion, 'his relation, Udayâditya, became king' and uplifted the earth taken by Karna.

claim.value: 'relation' (bandhu) of Bhoja, per Nagpur inscription as quoted by Ganguly

items.note: Ganguly: Udayāditya revived Paramāra authority in Malwa; 'He is described in the Udayapur prasasti as a relation of Bhoja.'

claim.value: described as a relation of Bhoja in the Udayapur prasasti

items.note: Udayapur (Bhilsa) inscription gives pedigree Sauravira, Gondala, Gyātā, Udayāditya, who recovered the interior of Mālava formerly governed by his ancestors.
Udayāditya and predecessors belonged to a junior branch, 'ruling as feudatories of the Imperial house of Dhārā, in the east of Malwa, at Udayapur, in Bhilsa'.
Ā'in-i-Akbarī story of Jitpal of the Tonwar caste elected to the throne; Ganguly says he 'is possibly the same as Udayâditya'.
Udayapur prasasti is engraved on a slab lying before the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple; the only record giving the complete genealogy from Upendra to Bhoja; undated, early in the reign.

claim.value: slab in front of Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple, Udayapur in Bhilsa; undated, early in the reign; complete genealogy Upendra to Bhoja

items.note: Two short inscriptions of Udayāditya's reign in the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple, one dated Sam 1137 = 1080 A.D.

claim.value: two short inscriptions in the temple besides the prasasti, one dated 1080 A.D.

items.note: Quoting Hall: Udayāditya 'is distinctly stated to have been ruling in Sam 1116, or Šaka 981'.

claim.value: ruling in Sam 1116 (Saka 981), per Hall as quoted

items.note: From inscriptions Udayāditya's kingdom extended to Jhalrapatan, Bhilsa and Nimar, regaining almost all of Bhoja's late-reign territory.
1086 A.D. Jhalrapatan record of Udayāditya's reign: a Śiva temple and tank built, with a promised annual gift of oil and sweetmeat.
Vikramāditya VI turned enemy and campaigned against Malwa; a 1077 inscription says he caused 'a great fever of terror to the king of Dhārā'.
Udayāditya engraved charts of alphabets and grammar rules on the walls of Bhoja's school at Dhāra and the Chauberdera temple at Un.
'He laid the foundation of the city of Udayapur in Bhilsa, and erected there the great temple of Nilakanthesvara.'

claim.value: Udayāditya laid the foundation of Udayapur and built the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple

items.note: An Udayapur inscription records the temple built in 1059 A.D., 'considered the most superb of its kind in the whole of India'.
Another inscription in the same temple credits Udayāditya with founding Udayapur, Udayesvara and Udayasamudra; 'Udayesvara is perhaps the same as Nilakanthesvara'.

claim.value: Udayāditya founded Udayapur, Udayesvara and Udayasamudra

items.note: 'At present, Udayasamudra cannot be identified. It must have been a lake or a big tank in the vicinity of Udayapur.'

claim.value: cannot be identified; probably a lake or big tank near Udayapur

items.note: Udayāditya reportedly erected many temples, excavated tanks, performed ceremonies and 'granted lands productive of gold and corn to the Brahmans'.
Ganguly's assessment: Udayāditya's 'career as a king was one of unique success', restoring peace and fostering literature and education.
'The great Nila-kantheśvara temple still stands to testify to his greatness'; Muñja and Bhoja's work continued under Udayāditya's patronage.
Rās Mālā tradition gives Udayāditya two wives and sons Jug Dev (Jagaddeva) and Rindhuwul (Ranadhavala).
Ganguly judges the Jug Dev story mythological and 'chronologically inaccurate', since Naravarman reigned before 1094 A.D.
Despite discrepancies, 'it cannot be denied that Udayāditya had a son named Jagaddeva, who, for some time, became the king of Malwa'.
Belava inscription of Bhojavarman states Jagadvijayamalla was the son of Udayi (Udayāditya); Śāstrī identifies him with Jagaddeva of Malwa.
Udayāditya's daughter Śyamala Devī married Vijayasimha of the Guhila family.
'Udayāditya closed his reign shortly after 1086 A.D.'

claim.value: closed his reign shortly after 1086 A.D.

items.note: Tradition names Jug Deb as successor, a Paramāra record names Lakṣmadeva; Ganguly conjectures Jagaddeva and Lakṣmadeva were one person.
The Nagpur stone inscription is the main evidence for Lakṣmadeva; he granted two villages on a solar eclipse, probably for a temple.
Nagpur stone inscription devotes nineteen verses to Lakṣmadeva's military excursions, a digvijaya like neighbours Vikramāditya VI and Karna.
Karṇa brought 'disgrace and ignominy on the Paramāras' in the mid-11th century, a wound Lakṣmadeva set out to heal.

items.note: Ganguly cautions that Lakṣmadeva's Pāṇḍya and Ceylon conquests lack corroboration and seem 'merely the panegyric of the poet'.
Nagpur praśasti by Naravarman has 58 verses: nineteen for Lakṣmadeva, three to Udayāditya and three to Bhoja; vague on predecessors' achievements.
Lakṣmadeva inherited a kingdom from Jhalrapatan to Bhilsa and Nagpur–Nimar, showing Paramāra power late in the 11th century.

items.note: Lakṣmadeva resisted Mahmūd's invasion of Malwa; 'the Moslems won some preliminary victories but were ultimately repelled'.
Naravarman-era slab found near a tank about a mile south of Udayapur records the tank's construction in V.S. 1151 = 1094 A.D.
Lakṣmadeva closed his reign before 1094 A.D. and was succeeded by his younger brother Naravarman.
Naravarman inscription on a pillar of the Bijamandira mosque at Bhilsa; Ganguly infers the building was originally a Carcikā temple converted to a mosque.
Madhukaraghar inscription names Naravarman's predecessors Sindhula, Bhoja and Udayāditya and records a Śiva temple dated Sam 1164 = 1107 A.D.
